newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece may scrap gene-tomato research.
newsitem.headline: Greece may scrap gene-tomato research.

text.p: Greenpeace activists dressed in tomato costumes extracted a concession from the Greek government on Tuesday that it would consider scrapping private research into genetically-altered tomatoes.
The Greenpeace protesters posted a sign outside the Environment Ministry reading "Ministry of Transmutations and Genetic Dangers" before meeting Deputy Environment Minister Theodoros Koliopanos.

They were asking the Greek government, which opposes the production, import and use of genetically engineered food, to rescind a permit granted to a private company in March to experiment with tomatoes to extend their ripening time and give them a longer shelf-life in stores.

After the meeting with Koliopanos, Greenpeace activist Nikos Charalambidis told Reuters: "The deputy minister said no new permits for genetically altered foods will be granted and that the government will examine the option of cancelling a permit granted to the Zeneca company for genetically altered tomatoes."
Ministry officials said Koliopanos had been concerned after his meeting with Greenpeace and was prepared to cancel the research permit if presented with new evidence that it was dangerous.
"The minister opposes genetically-engineered food. He signed this permit only for research but he is prepared to recall it," one ministry official said.
Greenpeace and other enviromental groups have launched an international campaign against gene-altered foods, such as soybeans and corn, saying they may have unknown health risks.
"We are used to protests about experiments on animals. It's time we protested about experiments on us," Charalambidis said.
Greek ministry officials said they considered research into the gene-altered tomatoes safe because it was kept within the controlled environment of a greenhouse.
But Greenpeace said there was no way of preventing the results of genetic testing in a greenhouse from reaching the environment because insects and pollen could not be stopped from interfering.
It asked the minister to ban the release of genetically engineered organisms to the environment and to work with other European Union countries to adopt strict measures against them.
"Greenpeace also asks consumers to pressure companies, supermarket chains and politicians to stop supplying markets with genetically engineered products," Charalambidis said.
More than a million Austrians have signed a petition calling for a ban on genetically modified foods, forcing a parliamentary debate on the issue.
